rentok.label: brand attribution fails by default and must be forced by name and package
rentok.claim: The default outcome, according to the source, is that a viewer remembers the commercial and forgets which product it was for, often attributing it to a competing brand. Registering the brand is therefore treated as work that must be done deliberately rather than as a by-product of a good commercial. His stated devices are to use the name within the first ten seconds and to play games with it, such as spelling it out; he reports a commercial that repeated the brand name twenty times without irritating anyone. Commercials that end by showing the package are reported more effective at changing brand preference than those that do not. He notes many copywriters think it crass to belabour the name.

rentok.label: demonstrations persuade but naming the competitor can make the competitor the hero
rentok.claim: Demonstrations showing how well the product performs are above average at persuading, and the source insists they need not be dull, instancing a paperboard bridge driven over by a truck and a glue commercial in which the announcer delivers his pitch hanging upside down by his shoes. He then states a specific and counter-intuitive failure of comparative demonstration: commercials naming competing brands were found less believable and more confusing, and viewers tend to come away with the impression that the disparaged brand is the hero. He notes the practice is illegal in Germany and encouraged by the United States government as consumer information.

rentok.label: show the product in use and in motion and repeat one visual device over years
rentok.claim: Showing the product in use pays, and where possible the end-result of using it — how a nappy keeps a baby dry, how pistons look after fifty thousand miles. For food the more appetising it looks the more it sells, and food in motion is said to look particularly appetising: chocolate sauce in the act of being poured, syrup over pancakes. Close-ups pay when the product is the hero of the commercial. Over a longer horizon he names mnemonics, a visual device repeated over a long period, which he says can increase brand identification and remind people of the promise.

rentok.label: draw on the full range of branding assets
rentok.claim: The source enumerates the branding assets available to a video ad — product shots, pack shots, in-situ branding, graphic elements, voice-overs and musical treatments — and asks for the brand identity to be worked into the story through a variety of them, selected to fit the message and the marketing objective rather than applied uniformly.

rentok.label: audio and supers reinforce the message without competing elements
rentok.claim: Audio and on-screen text are to be used to reinforce the story's key points, and the source attaches a negative condition to that instruction: competing elements are to be avoided. The two halves belong together — the reinforcement only works if the text, the audio and the picture are saying the same thing at the same moment.

rentok.label: a product can be built so that using it transmits a signal of its use
rentok.claim: The source's first constructive remedy for invisibility is to build the signal into the act of use, so that consumption itself broadcasts. His paradigm case is Hotmail's signature line appended to every outgoing message, which turned each user into a source of implicit endorsement to exactly the people they were already writing to. He generalises the move well beyond text: distinctive shape (the Pringles tube), sound (the Windows startup chime), unexpected colour (Apple's white earphone cords in a market of black ones, Louboutin's red soles), and enlarged logos. He notes this is disproportionately valuable to organisations with no advertising budget, because existing customers become the medium.

rentok.label: consideration objective weighting
rentok.claim: For a consideration objective, whose stated aim is to show users how the product fits into their lives, Attention is left at the core principles. Branding shifts to heroing the product. Connection carries two instructions, showing how the product works and being relatable. Direction is to plant the seed of urgency rather than to press for an immediate act.

rentok.label: open in the middle of the action or on a close up
rentok.claim: The source names two concrete opening constructions for an ad — beginning in the middle of the action, and opening on a close-up — and offers bold imagery at the start as a third means. It presents them as examples of many possible ways to earn engagement immediately, not as a required opening.

rentok.label: full funnel objective weighting
rentok.claim: The full-funnel row is the only one that gives all four principles an objective-specific instruction, and two of the four instructions are about ordering within the ad rather than about content. Branding is to start with a mix of branding elements and finish with the product. Direction is to use calls to action throughout the ad and to become more direct as it proceeds. Attention is to be hooked with audio while focusing on the elements that deliver the message, and Connection is to be established in support of the product.

rentok.label: the first frame decides whether the rest is seen and singularity is what sticks
rentok.claim: With thirty seconds available, the source treats the first frame as the gate: grabbing attention there with a visual surprise gives a better chance of holding the viewer, and commercials are screened out because they open with something dull. He states the asymmetry that makes this a real failure — the maker knows great things are coming and the viewer does not, and will have left before finding out. His instruction is literal: when advertising fire extinguishers, open with the fire. Alongside this he says visual banality fails, since a viewer exposed to thirty thousand commercials a year lets most slide off memory, so a commercial needs a touch of singularity, a visual burr that sticks; and he reports that commercials with a plethora of short scenes are on average below average at changing brand preference, conceding that one colleague handles many scenes without confusing people and that he himself cannot.

rentok.label: branded content must satisfy entertainment and marketing at once and its platform specifics are dated
rentok.claim: Sullivan's account of branded content has a durable core and a datable surface, and he marks the boundary himself in places. The core claim is that the work must satisfy two criteria at once: focus too much on the narrative and viewers may enjoy it without receiving any brand message, so the entertained audience must not leave without knowing the brand was involved. He states the strong form of the requirement — the idea cannot be a "brought to you by" attachment; it must come from and carry the brand's own material, and be relevant to the audience — and reports PJ Pereira's test: if it is impossible to talk about the idea without the brand, yet interesting enough to generate buzz, you have something. He records Edward Boches's participation sequence — do something interesting that communicates the brand's value, invite people into it, capture what they make, make it shareable — and notes the hard step is the first, which requires an idea worth advertising rather than an advertising idea. He states a bounding condition: whenever customers are asked for time or effort there must be a payoff commensurate with what was asked, or usage rates are very low. Everything platform-specific around this core — hashtag ceilings, which network's features to exploit, the stock-and-flow content vocabulary he footnotes as already out of use, the influencer arrangements — is contingent on the state of specific commercial platforms at the time of writing.

rentok.label: the customer is the hero and the brand is the archetype that enables them
rentok.claim: Sullivan proposes casting the brand as an archetype from the Hero's Journey and states the role assignment explicitly and against the usual practice: the brand is not the hero, the customer is, and the brand is the archetype the hero meets — the figure who teaches a lesson or grants a power before the hero returns transformed. He suggests the archetype's built-in character traits will start generating stories. Separately he reports two related compressions of a brand into a single part of speech: Dan Wieden's and Jean-Marie Dru's "brands are verbs" (IBM solves, Nike exhorts, Sony dreams) and his own "Brand = adjective" — the claim that a brand should be spot-welded to exactly one adjective and everything the brand makes should fall under it.

rentok.label: jump in reach the heart of the story faster
rentok.claim: The source's named technique "Jump in" asks the ad to reach the heart of its story sooner than it otherwise would, and names two specific means of doing so: pacing that keeps the viewer engaged, and tight framing.

rentok.label: direction ask for action with clear simple instruction
rentok.claim: The source's fourth principle is to ask the viewer to act and to make the instruction clear, concise and easy to follow. It names four vehicles that can carry that instruction — a written call to action, graphics, audio, or a scene from the story itself — so the direction need not be a caption at the end.

rentok.label: an idea without a conflict has no story to run on
rentok.claim: Sullivan holds that a brand story requires an opposing force, and that most briefs remove it. The common brief describes life after purchase — a world with no cavities, no breakdowns, no overdrafts — which he says cuts to the end of the movie and short-circuits the structure that makes a story hold attention. His stated diagnosis of an uninspiring brief is that it states a solution rather than a problem, and he says creativity happens in response to a problem, so a brief phrased as a solution gives the maker nothing to respond to. He offers a headline test for the same point: nobody reads "Area Bank Not Robbed", not because the reader is bad but because attention tunes out an unchanged status quo.

rentok.label: branding early often and richly
rentok.claim: The source's branding principle has three separate dimensions in one line: when the brand first appears (early), how often it recurs (often), and how many different kinds of branding element carry it (richly). The third is the one that distinguishes this from a simple frequency instruction — the source asks for variety of asset, not just repetition.

rentok.label: three television formats reported below average on brand preference
rentok.claim: Three formats are reported below average at changing brand preference. Celebrity testimonials fail because viewers guess the celebrity has been bought and are right, and viewers remember the celebrity while forgetting the product; the source reports the fees of the period to show what is being paid for. Cartoons can sell to children but are below average with adults, holding the viewer less well than live action and persuading less; he reports a fabric-softener case in which a cartoon commercial had no effect on a declining sales trend and a live-action commercial reversed it. Musical vignettes — a parade of fleeting impressions — he calls entertaining but impotent for selling.

rentok.label: engage with humour surprise and intrigue
rentok.claim: The source names three storytelling techniques as its levers for engagement — humour, surprise and intrigue — and frames them as emotional levers rather than as message devices.

rentok.label: recognising an idea that already has the traits is a separate usable skill
rentok.claim: Besides building stickiness into an idea, there is a second and separate skill: recognising an idea that already has it. The source's case is Subway's Jared campaign, built around an obese college student who lost more than two hundred pounds eating Subway sandwiches — a campaign the source calls a huge success, which came not from an advertising agency but from a single store owner who noticed the story.

rentok.label: search broadly before committing depth to any one direction
rentok.claim: Sullivan describes an explicit two-phase search. In the first phase the maker digs shallow holes all over the brief's territory — quick sketches, a billboard, a tagline, a script, enough only to show proof of concept — and does not stop to develop even a promising find. In the second phase, after a direction is chosen, the same idea is driven deep and pushed everywhere the brand meets people, which the agency he quotes extends past advertising into store design, uniforms, customer experience, internal communications and product ideas. He states the failure mode of skipping the first phase and the recovery when the second phase fails: an idea that looks huge can resist being enlarged, and the answer is to return to shallow holes.

rentok.label: dramatising the absence of the product beats dramatising its presence
rentok.claim: Sullivan states as a general preference that showing life without the product is usually more interesting than showing life with it, and names the strategist's term for the move: a deprivation strategy. He reports that got milk? was built entirely on this tension, each execution constructing a situation where the absence of milk is a small disaster, and he warns that briefs will repeatedly ask the maker to invert it back into the with-product form.

rentok.label: the failure is in the message not the product or the design
rentok.claim: When marketing does not work, the source's first move is to relocate the fault: not to the product, and not to the quality of the design, but to how the offer is described. Spending on design before the message is clear is presented as spending on amplification of noise.

rentok.label: three formats the trade dislikes that test above average
rentok.claim: Three formats disliked inside agencies are reported as above average at changing brand preference. Slice of life, in which one actor argues with another about a product in a setting approximating real life and the doubter is converted, has succeeded in case after case; copywriters detest it as corny and over-used. Problem-solution, which shows a familiar problem and then the product solving it, is as old as television. Talking heads, a pitchman extolling the product, are found non-creative by agency people and used anyway; the source says they are particularly appropriate for announcing new products, and instances a German cigarette launch where the only successful new brand among more than a hundred was launched by a talking head. He adds that reason-why commercials, which give a rational ground for buying, are slightly above average.

rentok.label: transforming the product image is a generator for visual ideas
rentok.claim: Sullivan offers a systematic visual generator: take the product and change it. Rotate it, invert it, scale it up or down, make its image rubber and stretch it, marry it with other visuals and icons, put a door in it, give it legs or a brain, ask what other thing it looks like, what could be substituted for it, and what the perfectly wrong way to use it would be. He states the constraint that makes it more than play: throughout, the maker is trying to coax out of the product a dramatic image with a selling benefit — the transformation must dramatise a customer benefit, not merely alter the object. He derives the exercise from watching a child reinterpret a toy car as a motorcycle, a boat and a rocket as it was reoriented.

rentok.label: direct response television needs length ordering time and several benefits
rentok.claim: Television that asks for a direct order is described as a different craft from television that builds a brand. The right kind of commercial sets up a problem and demonstrates the product solving it, gives a money-back guarantee, includes the price, and asks for the order explicitly and urgently. The demonstration should promise several benefits rather than one — and the source flags himself that this runs counter to the single-benefit formula he praises in his chapter on Procter & Gamble. Length is treated as a requirement: his most experienced colleague has almost never seen a commercial shorter than two minutes produce profitable sales, and twenty seconds must be allowed purely for ordering information, long enough to give a toll-free number and a post office box with supers and to repeat the number at least twice. He reports that long commercials seem to irritate people less than a cluster of short ones.

rentok.label: the seven element framework as the unit of message design
rentok.claim: The framework itself: seven elements — character, problem, guide, plan, call to action, failure avoided, success — which the source says are the necessary elements of a compelling story and the categories a brand message should be reduced to. It is presented as derived from studying hundreds of films, novels, plays and musicals, and as a summation of best practices refined over thousands of years of storytelling.

rentok.label: brand shows up early and throughout
rentok.claim: The brand or the product is to be introduced from the start of the ad and its presence maintained across the ad's whole length. The source treats these as one instruction: an early appearance that then lapses does not satisfy it.

rentok.label: action objective weighting
rentok.claim: For an action objective, whose stated aim is to present an enticing call to action with the right context, Attention is left at the core principles. Branding goes furthest here — "make the product the ad". Connection is to be exact and tangible. Direction carries an ordering instruction rather than a wording one: present the ask after the context has been set.

rentok.label: each piece must be self sufficient and must end by moving the reader
rentok.claim: Sullivan states two completion conditions that both follow from the same fact: the maker does not control the order in which a customer meets a campaign. Because there is no walking a customer through a portfolio saying which piece comes first, every single element must be completely understandable and whole in and of itself. And because a piece that resolves and stops leaves the reader at a dead end, every piece — web page, bill stuffer, video — should end with a call to action, whether that is finding more information, downloading something or joining a group.

rentok.label: humanise the story by featuring people
rentok.claim: Featuring people, and specifically people's experience of the product, is offered as the means of making the story humanly legible. The source attaches a representation condition to it: the people shown should represent the advertiser's consumer.

rentok.label: core abcds first then tailor to marketing objective
rentok.claim: The source states a two-stage decision rule. The core ABCDs are the starting point for any video ad; on top of them, the emphasis given to each of the four principles is then varied according to the campaign's marketing objective — awareness, consideration, action, or a combination of all three that the source calls full funnel. Across all four objective rows no principle is ever dropped: where an objective calls for no special treatment of a principle, the table's instruction is to apply the core principles for it.

rentok.label: awareness objective weighting
rentok.claim: For an awareness objective, whose stated aim is to get noticed, the source varies three of the four principles and leaves the fourth alone. Attention is to be won through audio — "pump up the volume by using audio to get viewers to pay attention". Branding is to be front and centre. Connection carries two instructions, making the people core to the story and being different yet simple. Direction receives no objective-specific treatment: the instruction is to apply the core principles.

rentok.label: a versus frame makes an open brief generative by narrowing it
rentok.claim: Sullivan reports that an unbounded assignment ("a campaign for Coca-Cola") stalls him, while the same assignment stated as an opposition ("a Coke versus Pepsi ad") starts producing ideas, and he recommends deliberately imposing the frame: draw a rectangle, put a line down the middle, let the line mean versus, and fill either side with any opposition that comes to mind — life with the product versus life without it, our product versus theirs, or a conflict borrowed from outside the category entirely. For a commodity where no in-category conflict exists, he says to go outside it, and demonstrates on bananas.

rentok.label: the brandscript as a single page message specification
rentok.claim: The framework's output artefact: one page holding the brand's whole message, with a named field for each element, created in the author's free web tool. The source instructs the reader to build one for the overall brand, then one for each division, then one for each product, and optionally one per customer segment — so the artefact nests across a company.

rentok.label: the consistency that produces the results is also what makes the advertiser predictable
rentok.claim: The source reports a detailed television practice — one important benefit promised, strategies unchanged for thirty years while executions are continually retested, a moment of confirmation in every commercial in which a user attests to the claimed property, demonstrations in sixty per cent of commercials, brand name in the first ten seconds and about three times thereafter, the promise delivered verbally and reinforced with supers and repeated at the end, unknown actors rather than celebrities as continuing characters, competitors referred to but never named, campaigns kept running ten years or more, budgets continually tested upward, advertising run all year rather than in flights. He then names the cost of the whole system: their Achilles heel is their consistency, they are always predictable, and it helps to win battles when the opponent's strategy can be anticipated.

rentok.label: the message must be structurally inseparable from the narrative
rentok.claim: The source's constructive rule, and the sharpest usable test in the book: the thing you want transmitted must be load-bearing in the story, such that removing it makes the story unretellable or unfunny. He applies the test destructively to his own favourite example — the Egyptian Panda cheese advertisements would be exactly as funny with a chicken suit and a used-car tagline, which shows the humour is not what does the work — and then shows the brand passes anyway, because the story cannot be told or understood without the panda. He applies it to Blendtec: it is impossible to tell the story of the clip that destroys an iPhone without saying that a blender did it, and without conveying that the blender is extraordinarily strong, which is exactly what the company wanted communicated.

rentok.label: connection make people think or feel something
rentok.claim: The source's third principle asks the ad to produce a thought or a feeling in the viewer, and locates the route to it in the experience of the product rather than in claims about the product. It names three things the ad can do to that end — educate, inspire, entertain — and frames them against a stated error, treating the viewer as passive.

rentok.label: deliberate collision with a distant subject domain and naming the idea before building it
rentok.claim: Sullivan reports Monahan's technique of listing forty or fifty data points about the brand's own subject, then building a second list from a subject chosen to be as far from it as possible, and connecting points across the two. He passes on Monahan's selection criterion for the second domain — familiar, unrelated to your work, and rich in data points — and his named rejects, which are unrelated but thin. Sullivan then offers a variant with the opposite setting: use a nearby domain instead, drawn from the truths of the product, category or customer, and use the collision to produce the campaign's name first, then write the campaign from the name. His stated analogy is coming up with the title before writing the book. He reports Thomas Kemeny on why the name matters operationally: it is the shorthand everyone uses internally and externally, what the client repeats, and how the press introduces it, and it should be telegraphic and clear about what the idea is. He is careful to note not every campaign needs one.

rentok.label: the customer is the hero and the brand is the guide
rentok.claim: The framework's central reversal, and the one the source calls a major paradigm shift. The customer occupies the hero role and the brand occupies the guide role. A brand that presents itself as the hero is competing with the customer for the same position, and the source describes the customer's reaction as recognising another hero and going back to looking for a guide.

rentok.label: replacing the key message with a key question that has no known answer
rentok.claim: Sullivan reproduces Tom Monahan's exercise as a three-stage ladder with a precise terminal condition. Question one is basic and has a correct answer, so no creativity is involved; question two is derived from the previous answer and can be guessed at, so some is; question three is derived again and has no correct answer that can be known or guessed, so creativity is required — and that is the better question. He instructs the first question always to be why people should buy the brand and the first answer to be the key message, so the ladder starts from the brief and climbs away from it. He notes the search is not linear: many threads dead-end, and the move is to back up, rephrase the last question and continue, which he demonstrates on two worked student cases. He then generalises it into a proposal about briefs: hand the creative team a key question rather than a key message, on the stated ground that a question has more potential energy because it is unfinished, where a message is fully cooked and asks nothing.

rentok.label: characters must be relevant and emotion is unquantified and needs a rational excuse
rentok.claim: A character used to sell a product over years becomes its living symbol and is above average at changing brand preference, but the source attaches a condition: provided the character is relevant to the product. On emotion he is explicit that researchers have not found a way to quantify its effectiveness and that his position is a belief formed from watching commercials: nostalgia, charm and sentimentality can be enormously effective, and emotion can be as effective as any rational appeal, particularly where there is nothing unique to say about the product. He then adds two constraints — consumers need a rational excuse to justify an emotional decision, so one should always be included, and emotion should not be attempted by anyone who cannot deliver it. He quotes a partner's warning that clients and agency people both overrate how much the rational benefits of their product matter to the consumer.

rentok.label: when every brand has a star the star must be cast as a character
rentok.claim: The author reports that the endorsement form changed once celebrity use became universal: a star simply declaring use of the product ceased to differentiate, so the star is now cast as a character within a story rather than appearing as themselves. He gives Preity Zinta in TVS Scooty as "just a girl having fun on her scooter", and Priyanka Chopra in Hero Pleasure playing a village girl who is underestimated by the man her parents have chosen.

rentok.label: demonstration outperforms assertion and can remove the need for a headline
rentok.claim: Sullivan states that telling people something is never as powerful as showing them, and draws a consequence about layout rather than only about persuasion: because the demonstration advertisement shows rather than tells, it does not need a clever headline. His strongest example inverts the usual relation between an advertisement and its medium — a magazine's own cover photograph, made with the advertised product, presented on the back cover with a line stating only how it was taken. He gives a second case where what is shown is the cause and the reader supplies the consequence: the mental image an anti-slip skate advertisement paints of children landing on their backsides, which he says is more powerful than showing them that way.

rentok.label: positioning is choosing two axes and going to their extremes
rentok.claim: Godin's positioning method is mechanical: draw two axes from attributes people care about, plot every available alternative on them, and take a position at an extreme rather than in the middle. The trade-off he attaches is the part with content. Choosing the axes most people care about puts you in a crowded quadrant, and in a crowded quadrant — without the magic of advertising — you cannot grow, because the customer does not know what to do and therefore does nothing. The alternative is to build your own quadrant from two overlooked axes and be the clear and obvious choice on them. He adds two modern conditions on the claims: they must be true and continually doubled down on in all your actions, and they must be generous, existing as a service to the customer, because the mid-century practice of inventing a differentiating claim does not hold up in a hyper-competitive world. And he names the cost: once you claim a story you are on the hook to deliver it — his music teacher now actually has to be more rigorous and to expel students who are not serious.

rentok.label: direct response print craft where the measure is orders rather than readership
rentok.claim: Restated for advertisements that ask for an order, the print rules change measure and in places change content. The headline is the most important element and the source reports seeing one headline produce five times as many orders as another. Long copy sells more, particularly for expensive purchases, and only amateurs use short copy. Cross-heads should be written so that skimmers get the main points of the sales story. Testimonials raise credibility and sales, and if one tests well two should be tried — but not celebrity testimonials unless the celebrity is a recognised authority on the product, such as a champion golfer on golf clubs. Copy should be black on white; he names two exceptions to his own reverse-type rule, theatre programmes read against the light from a stage and slides projected on a screen. Readers skip from the headline to the coupon to find the offer, so the coupon should be a miniature advertisement carrying the brand name, the promise and a small photograph. The received belief that clutter sells is reversed: he reports tidy, well-organised layouts increasing coupon returns.

rentok.label: attention hook and sustain with immersive story
rentok.claim: The source's first principle asks for two things, not one: attention must be hooked at the start and then sustained, and the means named for both is an immersive story built from audio and visuals together rather than a visual device alone.

rentok.label: a concept that makes more than one point makes none
rentok.claim: Sullivan states flatly that to create a simple advertising idea in any medium the maker must be limited to saying one thing, and that any advertising concept trying to make more than one point will not work. He extends this to the client request for a full-line advertisement: if a client has three important things to say, they need three advertisements, because customers shop for specific needs and never for a full line.

rentok.label: fast cutting norm has shortened the acceptable shot
rentok.claim: A very fast paced editing style, which some call the MTV effect after music video cutting, has become widespread, to the point where some producers and directors regard a shot longer than three seconds as boringly long. The source calls the development alarming while allowing that quick cuts can be very effective and have their place like all styles, and that what is acceptable in an action sequence is not acceptable in a love scene.

rentok.label: focus the message and avoid doing too much
rentok.claim: The source names doing too much in a single ad as a fault in its own right and prescribes keeping both the messaging and the language focused and simple. It places this instruction inside Connection, not inside Attention or Direction — on the source's arrangement, an overloaded ad fails to connect.

rentok.label: see and say audio brand mention reinforces onscreen branding
rentok.claim: The source claims an interaction rather than an addition: an audio mention of the brand raises the performance of the on-screen brand visual it accompanies. The instruction is to pair the two, not to choose between them.

rentok.label: product superiority verified blind and trial are stated as preconditions for advertising working
rentok.claim: Reporting the practice of the company he calls the most formidable competitor in his categories, the source records an ordering that puts advertising last. Superior product performance is the key, and if the consumer perceives no real benefit no amount of ingenious advertising can save the brand. Superiority is verified by blind in-home tests, so that it is apparent to the consumer rather than only to the maker. Massive home-delivered sampling comes before the advertising works, on the stated ground that the other elements of the mix become fully productive only once satisfied customers have had firsthand experience. Testing is patient to the point of six years in one regional expansion, and only three products in the company's history went national without at least six months in test market, two of which failed.

rentok.label: a message must name something the customer wants
rentok.claim: The framework's first required content: a specific thing the customer wants, defined in relation to the brand. Without it the source says the audience is never invited into the story at all, because wanting something is what starts a story and what the rest of it resolves.

rentok.label: a brand should own a visual territory recognisable before the content is read
rentok.claim: Sullivan reports Helmut Krone's requirement of a page style — that it should be possible to tell whose advertisement it is from twenty feet — and notes what is interesting about it: Krone was talking about print advertisements, not billboards. Sullivan endorses it and states a stronger version as his own view: the longer he has been in the business, the more convinced he is that art direction is where the major battle for brand building happens, because once a look is established and a design territory staked out, nobody else can use it without looking like your brand. He reports one instance of a look built by deliberate inversion of another: large pictures became small, small body type became large.

rentok.label: the gap between when you get bored and when they get the message
rentok.claim: Godin names a timing failure that follows from a memory claim. People remember what they rehearse — what they see and do again and again — and the market has come to associate frequency with trust, so the familiar is normal and the normal is trusted. The failure is that the maker's boredom arrives long before the audience's comprehension, producing what he calls a very real dip: you change the story exactly when the frequency was about to start paying, and never earn the trust. He quotes the rule that you change your advertising when your accountant is tired of it, not when you or your employees or your friends are, and generalises it beyond advertising to every kind of storytelling — new talks, new markets, new businesses abandoned just before the good part. He adds a decay claim: any tribal behaviour not energetically maintained loses half its activity, so persistence is not optional even after it works.

rentok.label: an identical offer can be framed to flatter rather than to humiliate
rentok.claim: The source reports a case in which the commercial terms were held constant and only the framing changed. A competitor sold women's garments by mail on instalments; the source set up a rival on identical terms, gave it a woman's name, pictured and signed the advertisements with a capable middle-aged woman, addressed the appeal from one woman to another, never mentioned instalments, spoke instead about credit and about what appearing at her best meant in a woman's career, and presented six months to pay as an accommodation rather than a concession — framed to resemble the thirty-day store credit that wealthier women received. It reports the new business dominated the field from the start and the competitor next door closed.

rentok.label: attention is given only to what reads as survival relevant
rentok.claim: The source's first stated cause of marketing failure. People continually scan their environment, advertising included, for information that helps them survive and thrive, and discard the rest. A message about the company's own history, scale or internal goals is therefore filtered out before it is considered. The source's illustration is that after an hour in a ballroom you would not know how many chairs it held but would know where the exits were.

rentok.label: abcd effectiveness lift claim
rentok.claim: The source attaches two effectiveness figures to the ABCDs as a set — a 30 per cent lift in short-term sales likelihood and a 17 per cent lift in long-term brand contribution — sourced to a study it names "The Short & the Long of ABCDs Effectiveness", credited to Google/Kantar, global, April 2021, with a sample of 11,000 ads. The publisher's three pages state the same two figures at three different strengths and with three different levels of citation detail.

rentok.label: the promise must matter to the buyer not to the advertiser and must be quantified
rentok.claim: In business advertising the promise must be important to the customer rather than to the advertiser, and the source's case is a software supplier proud of his company's size whose customers, on research, did not care about size and wanted responsiveness, support, service and a good product. The promise must also be specific: percentages, time elapsed, dollars saved rather than generalities. He extends this to a form of useful content — showing the reader how to calculate the money the product would save him — and reports that such an advertisement got the highest readership everywhere it ran and brought hundreds of requests for reprints.

rentok.label: the climax must convert present interest into an act before attention lapses
rentok.claim: The source treats the loss of half-made converts to procrastination as a standard and avoidable failure. A reader has paused because the subject or headline caught her; in a moment she will return to her reading and forget. The climax must therefore inspire immediate action among those interested. Its usual device is the coupon, and its stated reason is physical and behavioural rather than transactional: people cut it out, do not lay the publication aside, and the clipping travels — onto a desk, into a vest pocket — and resurfaces later as a reminder of something already decided, at which point it is sent for a sample or information and the interest can be followed up. It reports mail-order houses testing catalogue offers with and without coupons and finding an enormous difference in returns. It names other action devices — week sales, offers limited to a day or an hour, limited offers of every sort.

rentok.label: the resolved state must be stated not implied
rentok.claim: A message must say explicitly what the customer's life looks like after engaging the product, and the source calls this perhaps the most important element of a messaging strategy. Its examples are political slogans that named a destination and brands that state a resolved state — losing weight and feeling great, liking the way you look.

mokobara.label: engage with humour surprise and intrigue
mokobara.claim: The source names three storytelling techniques as its levers for engagement — humour, surprise and intrigue — and frames them as emotional levers rather than as message devices.

mokobara.label: attention hook and sustain with immersive story
mokobara.claim: The source's first principle asks for two things, not one: attention must be hooked at the start and then sustained, and the means named for both is an immersive story built from audio and visuals together rather than a visual device alone.

mokobara.label: draw on the full range of branding assets
mokobara.claim: The source enumerates the branding assets available to a video ad — product shots, pack shots, in-situ branding, graphic elements, voice-overs and musical treatments — and asks for the brand identity to be worked into the story through a variety of them, selected to fit the message and the marketing objective rather than applied uniformly.

mokobara.label: humanise the story by featuring people
mokobara.claim: Featuring people, and specifically people's experience of the product, is offered as the means of making the story humanly legible. The source attaches a representation condition to it: the people shown should represent the advertiser's consumer.

mokobara.label: show the product in use and in motion and repeat one visual device over years
mokobara.claim: Showing the product in use pays, and where possible the end-result of using it — how a nappy keeps a baby dry, how pistons look after fifty thousand miles. For food the more appetising it looks the more it sells, and food in motion is said to look particularly appetising: chocolate sauce in the act of being poured, syrup over pancakes. Close-ups pay when the product is the hero of the commercial. Over a longer horizon he names mnemonics, a visual device repeated over a long period, which he says can increase brand identification and remind people of the promise.

mokobara.label: characters must be relevant and emotion is unquantified and needs a rational excuse
mokobara.claim: A character used to sell a product over years becomes its living symbol and is above average at changing brand preference, but the source attaches a condition: provided the character is relevant to the product. On emotion he is explicit that researchers have not found a way to quantify its effectiveness and that his position is a belief formed from watching commercials: nostalgia, charm and sentimentality can be enormously effective, and emotion can be as effective as any rational appeal, particularly where there is nothing unique to say about the product. He then adds two constraints — consumers need a rational excuse to justify an emotional decision, so one should always be included, and emotion should not be attempted by anyone who cannot deliver it. He quotes a partner's warning that clients and agency people both overrate how much the rational benefits of their product matter to the consumer.

mokobara.label: audio and supers reinforce the message without competing elements
mokobara.claim: Audio and on-screen text are to be used to reinforce the story's key points, and the source attaches a negative condition to that instruction: competing elements are to be avoided. The two halves belong together — the reinforcement only works if the text, the audio and the picture are saying the same thing at the same moment.

mokobara.label: jump in reach the heart of the story faster
mokobara.claim: The source's named technique "Jump in" asks the ad to reach the heart of its story sooner than it otherwise would, and names two specific means of doing so: pacing that keeps the viewer engaged, and tight framing.

mokobara.label: a versus frame makes an open brief generative by narrowing it
mokobara.claim: Sullivan reports that an unbounded assignment ("a campaign for Coca-Cola") stalls him, while the same assignment stated as an opposition ("a Coke versus Pepsi ad") starts producing ideas, and he recommends deliberately imposing the frame: draw a rectangle, put a line down the middle, let the line mean versus, and fill either side with any opposition that comes to mind — life with the product versus life without it, our product versus theirs, or a conflict borrowed from outside the category entirely. For a commodity where no in-category conflict exists, he says to go outside it, and demonstrates on bananas.

mokobara.label: the message must be structurally inseparable from the narrative
mokobara.claim: The source's constructive rule, and the sharpest usable test in the book: the thing you want transmitted must be load-bearing in the story, such that removing it makes the story unretellable or unfunny. He applies the test destructively to his own favourite example — the Egyptian Panda cheese advertisements would be exactly as funny with a chicken suit and a used-car tagline, which shows the humour is not what does the work — and then shows the brand passes anyway, because the story cannot be told or understood without the panda. He applies it to Blendtec: it is impossible to tell the story of the clip that destroys an iPhone without saying that a blender did it, and without conveying that the blender is extraordinarily strong, which is exactly what the company wanted communicated.

mokobara.label: an object in transit licenses a move across a location
mokobara.claim: Technique 8.1. A minor object handed between characters — the example is a sheet of paper — gives the camera a reason to travel from one side of a location to the other. The object must be calibrated: not insignificant, but not the focus of the scene either. Both the start and the end of the move should be composed as though each were a finished shot in its own right, and the passage between them, where the actor moves past the camera, should be brief because it is not interesting enough to hold attention.

mokobara.label: the first frame decides whether the rest is seen and singularity is what sticks
mokobara.claim: With thirty seconds available, the source treats the first frame as the gate: grabbing attention there with a visual surprise gives a better chance of holding the viewer, and commercials are screened out because they open with something dull. He states the asymmetry that makes this a real failure — the maker knows great things are coming and the viewer does not, and will have left before finding out. His instruction is literal: when advertising fire extinguishers, open with the fire. Alongside this he says visual banality fails, since a viewer exposed to thirty thousand commercials a year lets most slide off memory, so a commercial needs a touch of singularity, a visual burr that sticks; and he reports that commercials with a plethora of short scenes are on average below average at changing brand preference, conceding that one colleague handles many scenes without confusing people and that he himself cannot.

mokobara.label: dramatising the absence of the product beats dramatising its presence
mokobara.claim: Sullivan states as a general preference that showing life without the product is usually more interesting than showing life with it, and names the strategist's term for the move: a deprivation strategy. He reports that got milk? was built entirely on this tension, each execution constructing a situation where the absence of milk is a small disaster, and he warns that briefs will repeatedly ask the maker to invert it back into the with-product form.

mokobara.label: open in the middle of the action or on a close up
mokobara.claim: The source names two concrete opening constructions for an ad — beginning in the middle of the action, and opening on a close-up — and offers bold imagery at the start as a third means. It presents them as examples of many possible ways to earn engagement immediately, not as a required opening.

mokobara.label: the seven element framework as the unit of message design
mokobara.claim: The framework itself: seven elements — character, problem, guide, plan, call to action, failure avoided, success — which the source says are the necessary elements of a compelling story and the categories a brand message should be reduced to. It is presented as derived from studying hundreds of films, novels, plays and musicals, and as a summation of best practices refined over thousands of years of storytelling.

mokobara.label: eye line match pays off a look with a correspondingly angled reveal
mokobara.claim: When a character isolated in frame directs attention outside its edges, the audience traces a line from their eyes to that edge and the filmmaker is then obliged to show what they are looking at. The revealing shot must be taken from a direction, angle and height closely matching the observing character's vantage. It need not be a direct point-of-view shot, but it must respect the established eye-line. The first shot sets up an expectation; the second fulfils it.

mokobara.label: the customer is the hero and the brand is the archetype that enables them
mokobara.claim: Sullivan proposes casting the brand as an archetype from the Hero's Journey and states the role assignment explicitly and against the usual practice: the brand is not the hero, the customer is, and the brand is the archetype the hero meets — the figure who teaches a lesson or grants a power before the hero returns transformed. He suggests the archetype's built-in character traits will start generating stories. Separately he reports two related compressions of a brand into a single part of speech: Dan Wieden's and Jean-Marie Dru's "brands are verbs" (IBM solves, Nike exhorts, Sony dreams) and his own "Brand = adjective" — the claim that a brand should be spot-welded to exactly one adjective and everything the brand makes should fall under it.

mokobara.label: a still reveal is a balancing act between delay and abandonment
mokobara.claim: The reveal is a cinematic device — the camera shows one thing, then moves or zooms to disclose something else, effective through surprise — and the source says it is difficult and perhaps impossible to achieve in a single still. The only approach is to arrange framing, composition or lighting so that attention goes immediately to one place, but the eye lingers long enough to start wandering and then discovers something else. It is an uncertain balancing act: hide the thing to be revealed too well — too small, too poorly lit — and the viewer will get bored and move on before noticing it.

mokobara.label: adding information does not change behaviour where the information is already held
mokobara.claim: The source argues that campaigns default to information and that information is the wrong instrument for the common case where the audience already knows the facts. Teenagers do not smoke because they believe it is healthy; people eating fast food are not unaware of the risks. Where the fact is already held, adding more of it changes nothing, and what is missing is the motivation to act, which is emotional. He extends the claim to categories with no obvious emotional hook, using Google's "Parisian Love" — a search interface demonstration built as a love story told entirely in query strings — as his case that any product can be given an emotional treatment.

mokobara.label: demonstrations persuade but naming the competitor can make the competitor the hero
mokobara.claim: Demonstrations showing how well the product performs are above average at persuading, and the source insists they need not be dull, instancing a paperboard bridge driven over by a truck and a glue commercial in which the announcer delivers his pitch hanging upside down by his shoes. He then states a specific and counter-intuitive failure of comparative demonstration: commercials naming competing brands were found less believable and more confusing, and viewers tend to come away with the impression that the disparaged brand is the hero. He notes the practice is illegal in Germany and encouraged by the United States government as consumer information.

mokobara.label: recognising an idea that already has the traits is a separate usable skill
mokobara.claim: Besides building stickiness into an idea, there is a second and separate skill: recognising an idea that already has it. The source's case is Subway's Jared campaign, built around an obese college student who lost more than two hundred pounds eating Subway sandwiches — a campaign the source calls a huge success, which came not from an advertising agency but from a single store owner who noticed the story.

mokobara.label: an idea without a conflict has no story to run on
mokobara.claim: Sullivan holds that a brand story requires an opposing force, and that most briefs remove it. The common brief describes life after purchase — a world with no cavities, no breakdowns, no overdrafts — which he says cuts to the end of the movie and short-circuits the structure that makes a story hold attention. His stated diagnosis of an uninspiring brief is that it states a solution rather than a problem, and he says creativity happens in response to a problem, so a brief phrased as a solution gives the maker nothing to respond to. He offers a headline test for the same point: nobody reads "Area Bank Not Robbed", not because the reader is bad but because attention tunes out an unchanged status quo.

mokobara.label: discontinuous shooting freed film from time and space
mokobara.claim: The discovery that certain kinds of cutting worked led immediately to the discovery that films could be shot discontinuously, which the source calls the cinematic equivalent of the discovery of flight: films were no longer earthbound in time and space. Discontinuity is the central fact of the production phase, and almost all production decisions relate to overcoming its difficulties or exploiting its strengths.

mokobara.label: alternating frame placement drives eye trace across the cut
mokobara.claim: The editor cannot compose the shots but chooses which compositions meet at a cut. Placing one character at frame left with open look room to the right, and cutting to a matching shot of the other character at frame right with look room to the left, makes the viewer's gaze travel across the screen at the cut and land on the new face. The source calls this eye-line match or eye trace and likens the effect to a tennis ball crossing a court.

mokobara.label: reciprocating imagery match coverage between characters
mokobara.claim: Coverage shot for one character must be matched by an equivalent frame for the other: the same shot size, and matched camera height, lens angle and angle on action, taken from the corresponding position on the opposite end of the arc. The editor should be given equal numbers of shots and matching framing for each character.

mokobara.label: consideration objective weighting
mokobara.claim: For a consideration objective, whose stated aim is to show users how the product fits into their lives, Attention is left at the core principles. Branding shifts to heroing the product. Connection carries two instructions, showing how the product works and being relatable. Direction is to plant the seed of urgency rather than to press for an immediate act.

mokobara.label: refusing the eye a resting place makes the image energetic
mokobara.claim: One of composition's prime jobs is keeping the interest going, so there are times when it is better to go against the expected practice of focusing attention clearly on one subject. Dividing the frame so the eye cannot rest anywhere for long produces deliberate disruption, and that makes the image more energetic. In the source's case the underlying division is still rectilinear, but set at an angle, with four faces of different sizes each in a squared-off segment keying the composition.

mokobara.label: when every brand has a star the star must be cast as a character
mokobara.claim: The author reports that the endorsement form changed once celebrity use became universal: a star simply declaring use of the product ceased to differentiate, so the star is now cast as a character within a story rather than appearing as themselves. He gives Preity Zinta in TVS Scooty as "just a girl having fun on her scooter", and Priyanka Chopra in Hero Pleasure playing a village girl who is underestimated by the man her parents have chosen.

mokobara.label: melodrama makes feeling exterior so setting and costume carry interior state
mokobara.claim: Dwyer argues that melodrama "foregrounds language, as it makes all feelings exterior," with characters verbalising their feelings, and that it likewise affects the image: it uses close-ups to increase the effect of emotional depth, and heightens the exterior display of emotion through storms, remote places and other symbolic representations of a character's interior feelings. She draws the consequence for settings directly: settings can be "a form of making the characters' state of mind external, following the melodramatic style of exteriority," and she reports Yash Chopra's own term for the resulting look, "glamorous realism," a style in which reality is glossed over to make it more attractive.

mokobara.label: a message must name something the customer wants
mokobara.claim: The framework's first required content: a specific thing the customer wants, defined in relation to the brand. Without it the source says the audience is never invited into the story at all, because wanting something is what starts a story and what the rest of it resolves.

mokobara.label: brand attribution fails by default and must be forced by name and package
mokobara.claim: The default outcome, according to the source, is that a viewer remembers the commercial and forgets which product it was for, often attributing it to a competing brand. Registering the brand is therefore treated as work that must be done deliberately rather than as a by-product of a good commercial. His stated devices are to use the name within the first ten seconds and to play games with it, such as spelling it out; he reports a commercial that repeated the brand name twenty times without irritating anyone. Commercials that end by showing the package are reported more effective at changing brand preference than those that do not. He notes many copywriters think it crass to belabour the name.

mokobara.label: an internal frame isolates one subject in a busy scene
mokobara.claim: An opening found inside the scene — a doorway, a window, a hoop — placed around one element directs attention to that element, and the technique is most useful precisely where the scene is otherwise disorderly. Carroll attaches an explicit condition: the device is powerful, so it must not be spent on an element that does not deserve it. He describes the result as a photograph within the photograph.

mokobara.label: a camera that ignores the action and arrives anyway reads as inevitability
mokobara.claim: Technique 8.5. The camera moves at a constant pace towards a close-up of one character, disregarding the objects and people moving in and out of shot, so that arriving there reads as inevitable — the source calls the sensation magnetic, with everything drawn into the moment. Two timing conditions are stated: the actor must end on a mark just in front of the camera's resting point, coming to rest with the camera or a beat or two earlier; and the actor must at first ignore the object entirely, because stopping when it is offered destroys the effect.

mokobara.label: branded content must satisfy entertainment and marketing at once and its platform specifics are dated
mokobara.claim: Sullivan's account of branded content has a durable core and a datable surface, and he marks the boundary himself in places. The core claim is that the work must satisfy two criteria at once: focus too much on the narrative and viewers may enjoy it without receiving any brand message, so the entertained audience must not leave without knowing the brand was involved. He states the strong form of the requirement — the idea cannot be a "brought to you by" attachment; it must come from and carry the brand's own material, and be relevant to the audience — and reports PJ Pereira's test: if it is impossible to talk about the idea without the brand, yet interesting enough to generate buzz, you have something. He records Edward Boches's participation sequence — do something interesting that communicates the brand's value, invite people into it, capture what they make, make it shareable — and notes the hard step is the first, which requires an idea worth advertising rather than an advertising idea. He states a bounding condition: whenever customers are asked for time or effort there must be a payoff commensurate with what was asked, or usage rates are very low. Everything platform-specific around this core — hashtag ceilings, which network's features to exploit, the stock-and-flow content vocabulary he footnotes as already out of use, the influencer arrangements — is contingent on the state of specific commercial platforms at the time of writing.

mokobara.label: direction ask for action with clear simple instruction
mokobara.claim: The source's fourth principle is to ask the viewer to act and to make the instruction clear, concise and easy to follow. It names four vehicles that can carry that instruction — a written call to action, graphics, audio, or a scene from the story itself — so the direction need not be a caption at the end.

mokobara.label: the face first then recognition a two stage account of why portraits open a poster
mokobara.claim: Patel argues that the star portrait is the natural opening component of a poster because it activates a "hierarchy of responses" in two distinct stages that she separates explicitly. First, an image of a human face is "instantly engaging because it is familiar to us all" — of any mix of images, the face is the one most likely to draw the glance, and this works WITHOUT recognition of the person. Second, and only within a specific cultural environment, the portrait is recognisable as a star, which arouses expectations built up over time. She states the boundary in the same breath: "an Indian film star will be unknown to the wider Western audience where his or her films are not so popular and the poster will not evoke the same response."

mokobara.label: screen position and attention persist when the other subject leaves frame
mokobara.claim: In a single close-up cut from a two-shot, a character must keep the screen position and direction of attention established in the wider shot, even though the other character is no longer visible in frame.

mokobara.label: frontality and iconicity as a freezing of space that renders meaning visible
mokobara.claim: Dwyer reports Geeta Kapur's formal category of "frontality" in the Indian popular arts and Kapur's use of "iconicity" — not in the Peircean sense of resemblance, but as a meaningful condensation of symbolic meanings into ONE STATIC IMAGE, which need not be religious or mythological. Frontality here is not merely filming from a right-angle plane or direct address to camera but also operates through the spectator's knowledge of narrative and mise-en-scene. Dwyer adds that frontality may be seen as a freezing of space, and sometimes of time, into a tableau, which positions characters and objects in relation to one another and gives the spectator "the opportunity to see meaning represented, emotions and moral states rendered in clear visible signs."

mokobara.label: story appeal in a photograph converts a glance into reading
mokobara.claim: The photographs that work hardest are those that arouse curiosity: the reader glances, asks himself what is going on, and reads the copy to find out. The source attributes the naming of this element to Harold Rudolph, who he says demonstrated a dose-response relation — the more story appeal injected into a photograph, the more people look at the advertisement. He names the Hathaway eyepatch as his own use of it, and states that if the subject of the illustration is not remarkable no photographer can save it.

mokobara.label: story structure lowers the cost of understanding a message
mokobara.claim: Story is offered as the specific remedy for processing cost, on the grounds that it is a sense-making device: it identifies an ambition, defines what stands in the way, and provides a plan, so the information arrives pre-ordered. The source's analogy is music against noise — the same sound waves, but organised under rules the brain can engage, which is why a song is remembered and a dump truck reversing is not.

mokobara.label: a package with detail on every side forces a narrower tonal range than a plain form
mokobara.claim: The source refuses to publish lighting ratios, on the grounds that the right amount of tonal variation depends on the subject and on taste. It nevertheless states the governing distinction. A simple cube with no important detail on any side can take the full range — black shadow, white highlight. A package that has to sell a product, with important detail on all three visible sides, cannot: the highlight must be only slightly brighter and the shadow only slightly darker than the third side, because detail in either extreme would be lost. The depth clue is thereby deliberately weakened in exchange for legibility.

mokobara.label: hard light simplifies by contrast and builds form by shadow
mokobara.claim: Hard light — one direction, high intensity — does two separable things. Its contrast makes anything in its path a highlight and leaves everything else dark, which can be used deliberately to simplify a composition: the shadows become large masses that mask unnecessary detail, and attention is driven to the lit parts. Its shadows have razor-sharp edges, and those decisive shadows create depth and three-dimensionality by describing the angles of what they fall across. Carroll also states the reciprocal reading: shadows disclose where the light is coming from and how intense it is. The cost is unavoidable and he says so — hard light is uneven, so detail is lost somewhere, at one end of the range or the other.

mokobara.label: each technique carries three image types with different evidential jobs
mokobara.claim: The source states its own visual apparatus. Frame grabs from named films show that the technique has been used successfully before. Overhead diagrams show where the camera and the actors move, under a stated notation: white arrows for camera movement, black for actor movement. A computer-graphics recreation closes each section, and the source states that these are deliberately not copies of the film frames — the differences exist to show that small changes to a setup extend the technique rather than break it.

mokobara.label: depth in a flat image rests on two clues perspective distortion and tonal variation
mokobara.claim: A photograph is as two-dimensional as a drawing, and the depth a viewer perceives in it is manufactured by two visual clues: perspective distortion, in which edges that are equal appear unequal and right angles appear not to be right angles, and tonal variation, the presence of both light and dark areas. The source demonstrates with a line drawing of a cube that lacks both clues and is not reliably read as a cube at all, and one with both clues that is. Lighting affects both: obviously through highlight and shadow, less obviously through the coupling described separately.

mokobara.label: see and say audio brand mention reinforces onscreen branding
mokobara.claim: The source claims an interaction rather than an addition: an audio mention of the brand raises the performance of the on-screen brand visual it accompanies. The instruction is to pair the two, not to choose between them.

mokobara.label: a story is a carrier and the information travels as cargo
mokobara.claim: The source's sixth driver is that people transmit narratives rather than facts, and that facts travel by being embedded in narratives people wanted to tell anyway. He separates the surface plot, which does the work of getting told, from what is carried inside it. His demonstration is an ordinary customer-service story about a replaced coat, which he unpacks into five separate pieces of usable information a listener acquires — about topcoats, down coats, that retailer's product, its service, and its behaviour when something goes wrong — none of which the teller set out to communicate. His second demonstration is the Subway diet: the fact that a chain has low-fat options is unshareable on its own, and the same fact travels freely inside a story about one man losing 245 pounds.

mokobara.label: connection make people think or feel something
mokobara.claim: The source's third principle asks the ad to produce a thought or a feeling in the viewer, and locates the route to it in the experience of the product rather than in claims about the product. It names three things the ad can do to that end — educate, inspire, entertain — and frames them against a stated error, treating the viewer as passive.

mokobara.label: awareness objective weighting
mokobara.claim: For an awareness objective, whose stated aim is to get noticed, the source varies three of the four principles and leaves the fourth alone. Attention is to be won through audio — "pump up the volume by using audio to get viewers to pay attention". Branding is to be front and centre. Connection carries two instructions, making the people core to the story and being different yet simple. Direction receives no objective-specific treatment: the instruction is to apply the core principles.

mokobara.label: flat light shifts the whole guiding burden onto composition
mokobara.claim: The flat light of an overcast day is very low in contrast, casts little or no shadow, and makes everything look flatter. Carroll draws the consequence that matters: with no dramatic shadows or highlights available to create depth and pull the eye, composition alone has to guide the viewer around the image. This is the one place in the book where he states an interaction between two of his chapters — the amount of compositional work required is set by the light. He also names the compensating gain: the resulting matter-of-fact quality draws the viewer in through unanswered questions rather than immediate effect.

mokobara.label: star identity as cumulatively built by three parties and carried by a few fixed features
mokobara.claim: Patel argues that star identity is not authored by the star alone but is "cumulatively constructed by the star, the artist and the public," so that a portrait carries "a concurrence of self representation, artistic interpretation, and viewer expectation." She then reports the pictorial consequence: the poster artist's aim is not the sitter's true identity, as in conventional portraiture, but "the 'mask' or the star's constructed identity," and a survey of the posters shows certain facial characteristics becoming the defining features that trigger recognition — for Bachchan, his heavy-hooded eyes, usually looking directly at the viewer or into the distance, and his full lips enhanced to impart a brooding air.

mokobara.label: full funnel objective weighting
mokobara.claim: The full-funnel row is the only one that gives all four principles an objective-specific instruction, and two of the four instructions are about ordering within the ad rather than about content. Branding is to start with a mix of branding elements and finish with the product. Direction is to use calls to action throughout the ad and to become more direct as it proceeds. Attention is to be hooked with audio while focusing on the elements that deliver the message, and Connection is to be established in support of the product.

mokobara.label: every departure from a shot must be motivated
mokobara.claim: Information governs the shot being cut to; motivation governs the shot being cut away from. There must always be a reason to leave the current shot and a reason it is left at that particular moment. The motivating element may be visual — usually some movement by a subject or object, from a car clearing a river down to a small shift of a character's eyes — or aural.

mokobara.label: brand shows up early and throughout
mokobara.claim: The brand or the product is to be introduced from the start of the ad and its presence maintained across the ad's whole length. The source treats these as one instruction: an early appearance that then lapses does not satisfy it.

mokobara.label: soft light flatters and hard light exposes
mokobara.claim: The choice between hard and soft light is governed by the photographer's intent toward the subject, not by taste. Soft light is less intense, so highlights and shadows are not starkly divided and shadow areas keep visible detail; its shadow edges fade rather than stop abruptly, which draws out form and features without severity, and it makes images feel slower and more contemplative. Hard light is the opposite instrument: unforgiving, exposing everything, and Carroll's instruction is unqualified — if you want to flatter a subject, avoid hard light altogether. He also gives the two ways to get soft light: diffuse the source, or in uncontrolled conditions simply avoid powerful directional sources.

mokobara.label: push the sharp element to the edge to send the eye to the real subject
mokobara.claim: An eccentric division puts the only sharp, strong element close to the frame's edge. The eye goes to it first, because it is the sole point of precision in the picture; but being so far to one side, the eye then has nowhere to wander except toward the true subject — in this case a pale, subtle storm above. The initial subject and the ultimate subject are deliberately different. The source adds that aligning the strong element exactly to the frame edge adds interest, and notes this was shot on film with no easy digital straightening afterwards.

mokobara.label: three white backgrounds and the manufactured ground shadow
mokobara.claim: Three white-on-white background types trade different things. On an opaque white background — the hardest case, because whatever is done to one affects the other — the subject is lit from above, which shades its front and fully lights the tabletop, and a gobo is then almost always needed to bring the over-lit top of the subject down to the tone of its front. The gobo is tuned by two coupled controls: closer to the subject makes its shadow harder, farther makes it softer but lighter, so a shadow that blends but is too dark calls for a smaller gobo and one that is too light for a larger. A medium-sized main light is recommended precisely to keep that adjustment available. The method fails on very shallow subjects — a white card on a white table cannot be shaded without shading the background equally. A translucent background lit from behind removes the coupling entirely, at the cost of erasing the ground shadow; the source then manufactures one, tracing a pleasing shadow cast by a test light onto paper, cutting it out, and gluing the cut-out beneath the translucent panel, so the apparent shadow becomes independent of the lighting of the subject. A mirror is the easiest white background of all, because it reflects almost nothing but direct reflection and those reflections are brighter than any diffuse white; it needs the largest light in the book, one filling the family of angles of the entire background, that light must show no texture because it will be sharply reflected, and no ground shadow is obtainable at all.

mokobara.label: a colour established earlier identifies a figure the frame cannot resolve
mokobara.claim: Technique 8.6. A character given a strongly contrasting colour can be identified even when blurred and distant, provided the association between the colour and the character was made in an earlier, closer shot. The source's example is an orange jacket in a frame graded almost entirely to blue, with a long lens close to the foreground actor letting the background blur. It states two constraints: an actor cannot be given a colour that does not suit the character, though contrast can always be introduced some other way; and the identification must be immediate, with no slow dawning.

mokobara.label: a two shot should be made active by moving the eye between the pair
mokobara.claim: The two shot — two people framed tight to medium so their faces dominate — is a classic of cinema and television, and widescreen suits it because it allows the pair to sit side by side with breathing space. Its point is the relationship between the subjects, so the composition should be managed to move the viewer's eye back and forth between them, making the shot active rather than static. The source's case achieves this with three devices working in sequence: selective focus and lighting put the eye on the foreground figure first, contrasting backgrounds — dark on one side, light and colourful on the other — carry it to the blurred but recognisable second figure, and the more dominant first figure brings it back.

mokobara.label: lighting level should follow the dramatic line across a whole film
mokobara.claim: In drama the lighting fluctuates across the film rather than being set once: gay sequences are lit brightly, sad scenes lower, and tragedy is served by strong contrast of deep blacks and glaring whites. The source calls the result a symphonic construction paralleling the dramatic situations, and says the purpose of a long shot in drama is not only geographical but to establish the mood and help tell the story.

mokobara.label: advertising style as a period marker and the authors own periodisation
mokobara.claim: Patel's organising claim for chapter 3 is that Indian film advertising did not evolve toward a single style but moved through distinct phases, each borrowing "the aesthetic vocabulary of the period." She sets out the sequence: text-only newspaper notices and handbills (1896 onward); the Ravi Varma aesthetic, realist oil technique applied to Hindu mythological subject matter, carried into posters via the Varma press's oleographs; the Bombay School of Art style, a delicate realism tied to Ajanta revival and used when a studio wanted to signal that a film was special; Art Deco from the 1930s as a universal symbol of modernity, which "did not survive beyond the end of the 1940s" in India because it was seen as Western cultural imperialism; nationalist imagery around Independence, often using the map of India; overpainted montage in the 1970s-80s; and computer-aided design from the 1990s.
